notes: The San Francisco Subjects Photograph Collection is the History Center's general subject file: 34,738 catalogue records filed folder by folder — parades, ferries, wildflowers, mayors — of which 1,435 carry a street number. Records that give no number are not kept as findings for this collection (COLLECTION_UNNUMBERED_POLICY in digitalsf_extract.py); the coverage block below records that the whole collection was read. The collection has no single creator, so a finding's description says only that the address was photographed, and names the building where the caption does.

record_notes: Printed on back: "Anshell & Allen, architects of San Francisco, have been awarded a 1962 Architectural Award of Excellence by the American Institute of Steel Construction for the design of the International Building, San Francisco. The jury praised the sophisticated plan developed from the air rights as well as its structural soundness in an earthquake area. The spirit of the Chinese environment in which the building sits was enhanced through the use of modern steel cantilevers. The building is adjacent to a public park and contains underground garage space for 1400 cars. Air rights were used to insure light and air on all sides and a connection with the park to the west. The 17-ft-length of the cantilevers was established as the maximum which could be attained without any premium in cost, and the cantilever established the basic outline of the structure.".

Printed on back (continued): "Owner: Natomas Company. Structural Engineers: Gould & Degenkolb and Robert D. Dewell. General Contractor: Dinwiddie Construction Company. Steel Fabricator: Bethlehem Steel Company. All are San Francisco firms.".

Ronald Smith (left) whose apartment is above that of the landlady, Mrs. Jean Toman, and Robert Mossberger (right) told of a ferocious fight between Mrs. Toman and her now dead tenant, Elinor Kahn. 'It was the worse I've ever heard,' said Smith. Mossberger told of a note he received from Mrs. Toman, asking that he pay his rent at once (extreme right). With the discovery of Miss Kahn's body, hacked and stowed in two suitcases, an all-points alarm went out for Mrs. Toman. She was seized this afternoon.".

record_notes: Newscopy: "Miss Alice Burr, who with her sister, Marian, inherited the tree-girt Allyne sister's Victorian house at 2609 Gough St., would like to see the property acquired by the city, either for the official residence of the mayor or for a public square. 'Either would be preferable to one of those big apartment houses,' Miss Burr told The News Call Bulletin. 'Naturally, I realize the City of San Francisco must build toward the sky, but I hate to see them rising all around us. While I'm not a worshipper of the past - in fact, I like to face the future - I'm selfish enough to want to keep the character of the city from changing too fast. I can't move my home - I'm too old now - and the bang, bang all day of the construction work would be most unpleasant.' The misses Burr live a block away at 1772 Vallejo St. Of the two proposals, Miss Burr would prefer to see the old Allyne house, where Lucy and Edith were born and lived out their lives, made the mayor's residence.".

record_notes: Newscopy: "San Francisco '49 Gold Rush celebrations, based on historical anniversaries, got under way today (February 28, 1949) with the centenary of the arrival of the Argonauts -- the first 'Forty Niners, 365 strong -- who reached San Francisco February 28, 1849 on the 'S. S. California.' The 100th  anniversary was marked by several civic observances today, including a brief ceremony at Fort Mason,   Port of Embarkation, commemorating the arrival on the 'california' of General Persifor F. Smith to relieve Col. Richard Barnes Mason as Pacific military commander. Impersonating General Smith is M/Sgt. James F. Warren. Paula Renz is a pretty modern representative of the first woman to reach San Francisco by steamer in the Gold Rush. Members of the Transportation Corps color guard are, left to right, Pvt. Charles Farthing, M/Sgt. J. H. Thompson, Sgt. 1/C J.H. Strader and Pvt. Harold Bullard.; Picture from: San Francisco Gold Rush Centennial Committee, YUkon 2-2700."

record_notes: Newscopy: "32 SCOUTS 'WORKING' WAY TO JAPAN--About 32 Bay Area Boy Scouts and half dozen of their leaders rolled out of their bunks this morning, on the way to Hawaii and Japan via a big Navy transport. They are paying their way to the Orient by standing duty en route, with daily inspection of their quarters. ALL BUT TWO of the 38 are Japanese-Americans--members of Explorer Post 58, and sponsored by the KONKO KYO (Shinto) Church at 1909 Church St. The boys will arrive in Japan July 11, tour the nation until Aug. 1, and arrive home Aug. ll aboard another Navy transport. A feature will be presentation to the Boy Scouts of Japan of an engraved plaque from the San Francisco Boy Scouts Council in recognition of their furtherance of world brotherhood. ABOUT 200 PERSONS were at Fort Mason, to see the Scouts board the Daniel I. Sultan. All of the Explorers, with the exception of Gary E. Utsumi, San Mateo, are San Franciscans. record_notes: Newscopy: "THIS OLD HOUSE at 600 Cambridge st. is reminiscent of days gone by at University Mound. In the background are new houses mushrooming on the 'mound,' replacing the rows of greenhouses. Although some flower-growers are still in business in the area, most have moved. On the 'mound' once stood Methodist College, later bought by James Lick for an old women's home. Many of the streets are named for famous universities, Harvard, Oxford, Yale, Amherst, Princeton, Dartmouth. Oldtimers at City Hall will tell you that for years this was one of the lushest potential residential areas in San Francisco, ideal for raising flowers and children. The flower growers happened to cash in first. But during the 20's, those wanting to rear families got interested in the rolling terrain, the climate, and the convenience of this land. Year by year, the offers got so attractive, that one after another, the nursery owner gave in. There are still some greenhouses, and some vacant lots, but they're going pretty fast..."
